title: tail repair discards a live reference and frees the item to the slab free list
consumer: items.c, do_item_alloc()'s LRU-tail branch under settings.tail_repair_time
live_proof: the branch is in the pinned tree at items.c:1117-1125, under upstream's own comment 'WARNING: This can cause terrible corruption', and is reachable in the shipped binary with -o tail_repair_time=N (N>=10, memcached.c:5291-5298). It was never fixed: 59bd02ce29 (2014-04-27) set TAIL_REPAIR_TIME_DEFAULT to 0 -- 'this feature does have a race for something grabbing active data from the tail' -- and the code stayed
object: an item, i.e. one chunk of a slab class, still referenced by a client
lifetime_ender: search->refcount = 1 followed by do_item_unlink_nolock (items.c:1121-1123), which takes the count to zero and calls item_free -> slabs_free; the chunk goes on its class's slots list (slabs.c:501), never to free()
shape: allocator-forced free of a referenced item / slabs reuse / read through the dead pointer
allocator_layer: slabs.c size classes over 1 MiB pages, memcached 1.6.45
fidelity: model-consumer, real allocator: slabs.c is upstream's file at the 1.6.45 pin through the port's two patches, and every allocation decision here is its own. The item layer is reduced to the three functions that decide whether a chunk goes back to slabs -- item_free, do_item_remove, do_item_unlink_nolock -- with their refcount arithmetic kept verbatim; the hash table, the LRU queues, the stats, the storage hooks and the locks are left out because none of them takes part in that decision
distinguishing: the other cases in this corpus are consumer mistakes -- a copy in the wrong order, a walk that reads a link it just returned. This one is the allocator's own escape hatch: the code deliberately overwrites the reference count of an item it knows is held, and upstream says so in the comment above it. It is also the only case here that is live in the pin
layer_note: tail_repair exists because refcount leaks used to strand items at the LRU tail forever. The cure frees them regardless of who is holding them; since 2014 it is off by default, and the stat that counts it (tailrepairs, items.c:807) is still reported

native-fix-differential.oracle: the buggy arm (tail_repair_time set) frees the held item, the next slabs_alloc returns the same chunk, and the holder reads the other item's bytes; the fixed arm (the shipped default) leaves the item alone and the holder reads what it stored
native-fix-differential.note: unit_reissued differs between the arms here, unlike cases 0 and 1: the premature free IS the defect, so the reuse it enables cannot be present in the control. That is why the case checks it before the marker

spatial.oracle: the sequence completes: report.completed == 1, no fault, the case marker printed
spatial.role: control for sublet: same binary and guest, one difference. A chunk keeps the alias it was carved with, so the holder's pointer still names live storage -- the next item's -- and the read succeeds

sublet.oracle: fault at the labelled read probe mc_defect_read, and nowhere else: exactly one fault, pc equal to the address the run's own marker published
sublet.note: release and issue each revoke the chunk, so the holder's pointer is dead twice over by the time it is read

poisoncap-spatial.oracle: the sequence completes: exit 0, report status=0 completed=1 count=1 mode=0, no fault observed by the supervisor, and the adapter's own line reports sweeps=0
poisoncap-spatial.role: control for poisoncap-protected: bounded leases and no invalidation, so the freed chunk stays addressable and the stale read succeeds

poisoncap-protected.oracle: fault at the labelled read probe mc_defect_read, observed from outside: SIGPROT with si_code PROT_CHERI_TAG, and the faulting address and the PC both equal to the address the supervisor resolved from the child's ELF and memory map
poisoncap-protected.note: si_code 2 and not 3: the sweep has run and the holder's alias is revoked, which is a different refusal from an access to a poisoned but unswept granule

cheribsd-revocation.target: stock CheriBSD purecap with libc revocation on
cheribsd-revocation.oracle: MEASURED 2026-10-06 on this host: the sequence COMPLETES. exit=0, completed=1, object_reuses=0, chunk_reuses=1. Not caught. The reuse counters are the point: the storage really was handed back out, which is the situation revocation would have to catch if the memory reached free(). It does not -- cache.c keeps it on its own STAILQ and slabs.c returns it to the page, so libc's quarantine never holds it. EVIDENCE COMMITTED 2026-10-06: results/20261006-cheribsd/. Both controls are in that bundle -- the revocation control FAULTED with addr == pc == the independently resolved expectation (0x101e42), proving the revoker sweeps in this guest AND attributing the fault; and a NEGATIVE CONTROL run on the same vehicle makes all 8 case oracles FAIL while the three platform controls still pass, so none of these completions is vacuous. The image hash is byte-identical to the vehicle the ffmpeg readings of the same day used, so the two programs' columns are comparable.
cheribsd-revocation.control: the control fired in the SAME boot: revocation-control exit=162 signal=34 (SIGPROT) si_code=2 (PROT_CHERI_TAG) with pc == the address the supervisor resolved independently (0x101e42). The platform controls cheribsd-abi and cheribsd-bounds passed in the same run.
cheribsd-revocation.platform: stock CheriBSD purecap built on this host with tests/cheri-baseline/provision-cheri-vehicle.sh (kernel CHERI-PURECAP-QEMU, releng/26.07-88f39900c329 = pins.env's CHERIBSD_REV; hw.machine_arch riscv64c; qemu 16135483052dfdd6, firmware f0e1fe57b0f85075, kernel 8ab453f46dc76cf2, libc fdce2289224bb519, image 0cb16209c16c5edf). NOT the PoisonCap platform the 2026-09-21 bundles used, so those hashes differ by construction.

native-detect.requires: the chunk never reaches free(), so ASan has no event; it would see the reuse only as an ordinary live object

note: damage is the holder reading another item's bytes where it stored its own. Upstream's warning says 'terrible corruption' without naming a consequence; this records the step that produces it
nested_why: memcached's slab allocator carved the object out of a 1 MiB page it owns -- so under this inventory's axis, WHO ALLOCATED THE OBJECT, this row is NESTED.
